contenu_vulgarise:
New Haven, 1961. One participant plays the “teacher.” Another, in the next room, plays the “learner.” At each mistake, the teacher must administer an electric shock of increasing intensity. The learner is in fact an actor, and the shocks do not exist.

From a certain level, the learner protests, screams, begs, then goes silent. An experimenter in a lab coat repeats prods: “please continue,” “the experiment requires that you continue.”

In the best-known version, about 65% of participants go all the way to the last switch.

## Why It Holds Up Better Than Others

Unlike the Stanford experiment, Milgram's has been reproduced, in several countries, and up to recent versions compliant with current ethical rules. The rates vary, the order of magnitude holds. This is not a fragile study.

The difference from the Stanford experiment deserves to be stated: one collapses when the archives are opened, the other comes out complicated but standing. Not all famous experiments have the same status, and treating them as a block would be as lazy as taking them on faith.

What is being qualified today is not the result. It is its interpretation.

## What the Archives Add

Milgram's documents, studied notably by the psychologist Gina Perry, show first that “the experiment” is not one. It is a series of twenty-four variants, whose obedience rates range from almost zero to more than 90%. The famous 65% corresponds to one configuration among others.

They show next that the experimenter improvised, sometimes insisting well beyond the four prods provided for by the protocol. And that a not insignificant number of participants doubted the reality of the shocks.

Above all, the variants say something precise. Obedience collapses as soon as the experimenter gives his orders by telephone, as soon as the victim is in the same room, or as soon as another “teacher” refuses first.

## What This Shifts

The usual interpretation, we blindly obey authority, is too flat to account for these gaps. The variants show people who negotiate, hesitate, look for reasons, and stop obeying as soon as they are given one.

A more recent reading puts it differently: participants do not so much submit as buy into a project that is presented to them as scientific and legitimate. It is not fear of authority that holds them. It is the feeling of taking part in something useful.

That is markedly less reassuring.

carte.punch: “Milgram” is not one experiment. It is twenty-four variants.
carte.idee: Obedience rates range from almost zero to more than 90% depending on the configuration. Obedience collapses if the order comes by telephone, if the victim is in the same room, or if someone else refuses first.

quiz.question: What do the twenty-four variants of Milgram's experiment reveal?
choix: That the 65% rate was a calculation error, since corrected
That almost all participants knew the shocks were fake
That the result could never be reproduced by other teams
That obedience varies enormously with conditions, from almost zero to more than 90%
quiz.explication: The result itself has indeed been reproduced, including recently. It is the variants that complicate the interpretation: obedience drops when the order comes by telephone, when the victim is visible, or when a peer refuses first. People who blindly obey would not react to such details.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What do the archives studied by Gina Perry show about the experimenter's behavior?
choix: That he merely read the four prescribed prods, never saying more
That he improvised, sometimes insisting well beyond the four prods provided for by the protocol
That he himself did not know whether the shocks administered were real
That he switched roles with the participant midway through the experiment
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The documents studied by Gina Perry show that the experimenter improvised, sometimes going well beyond the four prods provided for by the official protocol, which qualifies the rigor of the experiment.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Under what conditions does obedience collapse, according to the variants studied?
choix: When the experimenter wears a white coat rather than a suit
When the session takes place in the afternoon rather than the morning
When the participant is paid for taking part
When the orders come by telephone, or when the victim is in the same room
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Obedience collapses as soon as the experimenter gives his orders by telephone, as soon as the victim is in the same room as the participant, or as soon as another teacher refuses first to obey.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How does Milgram's experiment differ from the Stanford one, according to the entry?
choix: Milgram's was reproduced in several countries and holds up under examination of the archives, unlike Stanford's
Milgram's was run on a much larger sample of participants
Milgram's archives have never been subjected to critical examination
Milgram's was funded by a different, more rigorous institution
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Unlike the Stanford experiment, which collapses when its archives are opened, Milgram's has been reproduced in several countries, including recently, and comes out complicated but standing.
